{{Short description|Physics equation for velocity}}
{{Other uses|Torricelli (disambiguation){{!}}Torricelli}}
{{more citations needed|date=May 2021}}

In physics, '''Torricelli's equation''', or '''Torricelli's formula''', is an equation created by [[Evangelista Torricelli]] to find the final [[velocity]] of a moving object with [[Acceleration#Uniform acceleration|constant acceleration]] along an axis (for example, the ''x'' axis) without having a known time interval.

The equation itself is<ref name="Bertoldo2008">{{cite book |author=Leandro Bertoldo |title=Fundamentos do Dinamismo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cX1JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA41 |date=2008 |location=[[Joinville]] |publisher=[[Clube de Autores]] |pages=41–42 |language=Portuguese}}</ref>
<math display="block">
 v_\text{f}^2 = v_\text{i}^2 + 2a\Delta x,
</math>
where
: <math>v_\text{f}</math> is the object's final [[velocity]] along the ''x'' axis on which the acceleration is constant,
: <math>v_\text{i}</math> is the object's initial velocity along the ''x'' axis,
: <math>a</math> is the object's [[acceleration]] along the ''x'' axis, which is given as a constant,
: <math>\Delta x</math> is the object's change in position along the ''x'' axis, also called [[Displacement (vector)|displacement]].

In this and all subsequent equations in this article, the subscript <math>x</math> (as in <math>{v_\text{f}}_x</math>) is implied, but is not expressed explicitly for clarity in presenting the equations.

This equation is valid along any axis on which the acceleration is constant.

== Derivation ==

=== Without differentials and integration ===

Begin with the following relations for the case of uniform acceleration:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">x_\text{f} - x_\text{i} = v_\text{i}t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">v_\text{f} - v_\text{i} = at </math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

Take {{EquationNote|1|(1)}}, and multiply both sides with acceleration <math display="inline">a</math>

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = av_\text{i}t + \tfrac{1}{2}a^2t^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

The following rearrangement of the right hand side makes it easier to recognize the coming substitution:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = v_\text{i}(at) + \tfrac{1}{2}(at)^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}

Use {{EquationNote|2|(2)}} to substitute the product <math display="inline">at</math>:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = v_\text{i} (v_\text{f} - v_\text{i}) + \tfrac{1}{2}(v_\text{f} - v_\text{i})^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

Work out the multiplications:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = v_\text{i} v_\text{f} - v_\text{i}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{f}^2 - v_\text{i} v_\text{f} + \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}

The crossterms <math display="inline">v_\text{i}v_\text{f}</math> drop away against each other, leaving only squared terms:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{f}^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}

{{EquationNote|7|(7)}} rearranges to the form of Torricelli's equation as presented at the start of the article:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">v_\text{f}^2 = v_\text{i}^2 + 2a\Delta x</math>|{{EquationRef|8}}}}

=== Using differentials and integration ===
Begin with the definitions of velocity as the derivative of the position, and acceleration as the derivative of the velocity:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">v = \frac{dx}{dt} </math>|{{EquationRef|9}}}}

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a = \frac{dv}{dt} </math>|{{EquationRef|10}}}}

Set up integration from initial position <math display="inline">x_\text{i}</math> to final position <math display="inline">x_\text{f}</math>

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}}a\,dx </math>|{{EquationRef|11}}}}

In accordance with {{EquationNote|9|(9)}} we can substitute <math display="inline">dx</math> with <math display="inline">v\,dt</math>, with corresponding change of limits.

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{t_\text{i}}^{t_\text{f}} a\,v\,dt </math>|{{EquationRef|12}}}}

Here changing the order of <math display="inline">a</math> and <math display="inline">v</math> makes it easier to recognize the upcoming substitution.

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{t_\text{i}}^{t_\text{f}} v\,a\,dt </math>|{{EquationRef|13}}}}

In accordance with {{EquationNote|10|(10)}} we can substitute <math display="inline">a\,dt</math> with <math display="inline">dv</math>, with corresponding change of limits.

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{v_\text{i}}^{v_\text{f}} v\,dv </math>|{{EquationRef|14}}}}

So we have:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}} a\,dx=\int_{v_\text{i}}^{v_\text{f}}v\,dv </math>|{{EquationRef|15}}}}

Since the acceleration is constant, we can factor it out of the integration:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}}dx=\int_{v_\text{i}}^{v_\text{f}}v\,dv </math>|{{EquationRef|16}}}}

Evaluating the integration:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a x\Big|_{x=x_\text{i}}^{x=x_\text{f}} = \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \Big|_{v=v_\text{i}}^{v=v_\text{f}} </math>|{{EquationRef|17}}}}

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a \left(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2} \left(v_\text{f}^2 - v_\text{i}^2\right) </math>|{{EquationRef|18}}}}

The factor <math display="inline">x_\text{f}-x_\text{i}</math> is the displacement <math display="inline">\Delta x</math>:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">2a\Delta x=v_\text{f}^2-v_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|19}}}}

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">v_\text{f}^2=v_\text{i}^2+2a\Delta x</math>|{{EquationRef|20}}}}

== Application ==

Combining Torricelli's equation with <math display="inline">F=ma</math> gives the work-energy theorem.

Torricelli's equation and the generalization to non-uniform acceleration have the same form:

Repeat of {{EquationNote|16|(16)}}:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}}a\,dx=\int_{v_\text{i}}^{v_\text{f}}v\,dv </math>|{{EquationRef|21}}}}

Evaluating the right hand side:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}} a\,dx=\tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{f}^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|22}}}}

To compare with Torricelli's equation: repeat of {{EquationNote|7|(7)}}:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a(x_\text{f} - x_\text{i}) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{f}^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|23}}}}

To derive the [[Work (physics)|work-energy theorem]]: start with <math display="inline">F=ma</math> and on both sides state the integral with respect to the position coordinate. If both sides are integrable then the resulting expression is valid:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}} F\,dx = \int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}} ma\,dx </math>|{{EquationRef|24}}}}

Use {{EquationNote|22|(22)}} to process the right hand side:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\int_{x_\text{i}}^{x_\text{f}} F\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_\text{f}^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_\text{i}^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|25}}}}


The reason that the right hand sides of {{EquationNote|22|(22)}} and {{EquationNote|23|(23)}} are the same:

First consider the case with two consecutive stages of different uniform acceleration, first from <math display="inline">s_0</math> to <math display="inline">s_1</math>, and then from <math display="inline">s_1</math> to <math display="inline">s_2</math>.

Expressions for each of the two stages:

<math display="block">a_1(s_1-s_0) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_1^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_0^2</math>
<math display="block">a_2(s_2-s_1) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_2^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_1^2</math>

Since these expressions are for consecutive intervals they can be added; the result is a valid expression.

Upon addition the intermediate term <math display="inline">\tfrac{1}{2}v_1^2</math> drops out; only the outer terms <math display="inline">\tfrac{1}{2}v_2^2</math> and <math display="inline">\tfrac{1}{2}v_0^2</math> remain:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">a_1(s_1-s_0) + a_2(s_2-s_1) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_2^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_0^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|26}}}}

The above result generalizes: the total distance can be subdivided into any number of subdivisions; after adding everything together only the outer terms remain; all of the intermediate terms drop out.

The generalization of {{EquationNote|26|(26)}} to an arbitrary number of subdivisions of the total interval from <math display="inline">s_0</math> to <math display="inline">s_n</math> can be expressed as a summation:

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^n a_\text{i}(s_\text{i} - s_{i-1}) = \tfrac{1}{2}v_n^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_{i-1}^2</math>|{{EquationRef|27}}}}
